title: Pretraining: Data, Scaling, and Reliable Execution
summary: Design a defensible pretraining program by connecting corpus construction, tokenization, compute allocation, inference demand, and recoverable distributed execution.
learningObjectives: Specify a reproducible corpus pipeline and distinguish duplicates from benchmark contamination.
Calculate token budgets, mixture exposure, training FLOPs, and lifecycle break-even points.
Explain when empirical scaling fits stop supporting an extrapolation.
Choose parallelism and checkpoint boundaries that preserve training progress.

sections.title: 1. Treat the corpus as a versioned training dependency
paragraphs: Autoregressive pretraining minimizes next-token cross-entropy over a chosen distribution of sequences. The model learns whatever repeatedly reduces that objective: useful reasoning patterns, formatting conventions, factual associations, and unwanted shortcuts. A trillion-token counter describes exposure, not information quality. Start an interview answer by naming the target languages, domains, downstream tasks, training budget, and permitted data sources. Those choices define what useful pretraining means.

A practical pipeline ingests source snapshots, extracts text, applies quality and policy filters, removes redundancy, assigns evaluation partitions, tokenizes, and writes immutable training shards. Record source identifiers, acquisition dates, transformation versions, rejection reasons, and checksums in a manifest. Make rejected-document samples inspectable. A quality classifier can silently select a narrow writing style; manual stratified audits should examine what disappears as well as what survives. RefinedWeb provides evidence that carefully processed web data can be valuable, but does not establish one universal filtering recipe.

For an original planning example, suppose a crawl contains 1,000 billion estimated tokens. Extraction retains 80%, quality filtering retains 75% of that remainder, and deduplication retains 70%. The result is 420 billion tokens, not 1,000 minus 20 minus 25 minus 30 percent of the original. These rates depend on stage order. Recompute actual token counts after fixing the tokenizer, then reserve evaluation partitions and operational headroom before promising a training horizon.

sections.title: 2. Separate redundancy, contamination, and legitimate repetition
paragraphs: Exact deduplication hashes normalized documents; near-duplicate methods compare approximate fingerprints of overlapping text. Paragraph or substring checks catch repeated boilerplate that document hashes miss. Normalization must be domain aware: deleting punctuation might merge distinct programs or equations. Choose the survivor deliberately, retaining provenance for the entire cluster. Deduplication research shows reduced memorization and improved evaluation validity; it does not imply that every repeated phrase should be removed.

Contamination is evaluation information entering training, including copied questions, answer explanations, translations, and benchmark-derived tutorials. Deduplicating training documents alone cannot prevent it. Compare candidate data with protected evaluation material, split related document families together, and retain source or time holdouts where possible. Similarity thresholds create false positives and false negatives; report the method and suspicious overlap instead of claiming perfect cleanliness. A model may also have learned a fact legitimately even when a benchmark later asks about it.

Consider 100 benchmark questions, of which 20 have near-identical solved examples in the corpus. If accuracy is 95% on those 20 and 60% on the remaining 80, aggregate accuracy is 67%. The clean subset is still only 60%, and the seven-point increase cannot safely be credited to generalization. This arithmetic is illustrative, not a causal contamination estimate: the two subsets may differ in difficulty. Preserve both stratified scores and a newly constructed holdout.

sections.title: 3. Tokenization changes the budget and the effective curriculum
paragraphs: A tokenizer maps text to the discrete IDs predicted by the model. Subword schemes trade vocabulary size against sequence length; SentencePiece demonstrates training subword tokenizers directly from raw sentences without requiring language-specific word segmentation. Tokenizer normalization, byte handling, special tokens, and reversible decoding are part of the model interface. Freeze them before the main run. Changing token IDs afterward invalidates the learned embedding and output interpretation unless an explicit migration is trained.

Measure compression separately for each target language, code, and numeric text. In an illustrative corpus, a language requiring two tokens per word occupies twice the context positions of one requiring one token per word. Equal token allocation then delivers unequal word exposure. Bigger vocabularies can shorten sequences but increase embedding and output-layer costs; token-level perplexities across tokenizers are not directly comparable. Use a common text-level normalization, such as bits per byte, plus downstream tasks when comparing tokenization choices.

Mixture weights describe sampling probabilities, not corpus ownership. Suppose a 300B-token run allocates 50% web, 30% code, and 20% technical text. Expected exposures are 150B, 90B, and 60B tokens. If the technical corpus contains only 15B unique tokens, it receives four nominal passes while a much larger web corpus might receive less than one. Log unique coverage and repeat counts by domain. Oversampling can improve a target domain while increasing memorization or degrading other domains; choose weights through controlled ablations with the same evaluation protocol.
sections.formula: Expected exposure Dᵢ = pᵢD; nominal passes eᵢ = pᵢD / Uᵢ, where Uᵢ is unique tokens

sections.title: 4. Allocate compute with a fitted model, then test its assumptions
paragraphs: An empirical scaling law predicts held-out cross-entropy from quantities such as parameter count N and token exposures D. A common fitted form is E + A/N^α + B/D^β, with coefficients tied to a particular data distribution, architecture family, and training recipe. For dense transformers, C ≈ 6ND estimates training floating-point operations when parameter matrix multiplications dominate. It omits important costs such as long-context attention, recomputation, and communication. Chinchilla found approximately balanced scaling of parameters and data as training compute grows; a fixed tokens-per-parameter ratio is a planning heuristic, not a law of nature.

For an original budget example, N = 7 × 10⁹ parameters and D = 140 × 10⁹ token exposures give C ≈ 5.88 × 10²¹ FLOPs. At a sustained aggregate model-compute rate of 2 × 10¹⁵ FLOP/s, the idealized duration is 2.94 million seconds, about 34 days. This sustained rate is an assumption, not a hardware specification. Startup, checkpoints, outages, and evaluations extend calendar time. If the usable compute budget quadruples and a locally fitted frontier scales both N and D with the square root of compute, the corresponding candidate is 14B parameters and 280B tokens.

Before approving that candidate, run several smaller model sizes at several training horizons, with learning-rate schedules matched to each horizon. Hold out runs from fitting and inspect prediction errors. Compare measured throughput as well as loss: an awkward tensor shape may lose more wall-clock efficiency than its FLOP estimate suggests. Reserve some budget for these experiments; otherwise a precise-looking extrapolation can conceal a poorly chosen data recipe.
sections.formula: L(N,D) ≈ E + A/N^α + B/D^β; Ctrain ≈ 6ND; elapsed seconds ≈ Ctrain / sustained FLOP/s

sections.title: 5. Training efficiency and serving efficiency have different optima
paragraphs: A training-optimal model minimizes loss for a training budget. A deployed model must also meet quality, latency, memory, and lifetime serving constraints. Inference-aware scaling work explicitly includes anticipated inference demand and can favor training a smaller model longer. The decision requires comparable quality; simply comparing a weak small model with a capable large model is not an economic optimization.

Consider two hypothetical candidates that have already met the same evaluation gate. Candidate A has 10B parameters and trains on 200B tokens, costing approximately 1.2 × 10²² FLOPs. Candidate B has 5B parameters and trains on 800B tokens, costing 2.4 × 10²² FLOPs. With a deliberately simplified inference cost of 2N FLOPs per processed token, B saves 10¹⁰ FLOPs per token. Its extra 1.2 × 10²² training FLOPs break even after 1.2 × 10¹² inference tokens. Below that demand, A wins on this narrow total-FLOP calculation; above it, B wins.

Real serving costs require workload measurements. Prompt processing and autoregressive decoding stress hardware differently; context length changes attention work and KV-cache memory, and batching changes utilization. Dollar cost is not a constant multiple of FLOPs. Translate the forecast into input/output length distributions, concurrency, latency targets, and deployment duration, then benchmark candidate serving configurations. Treat demand uncertainty as a range and recalculate the decision at its endpoints.
sections.formula: Qbreak-even = (Ctrain,B − Ctrain,A) / (cinfer,A − cinfer,B), assuming equal acceptable quality

sections.title: 6. Map the training state and communication onto the cluster
paragraphs: Data parallelism processes different samples on model replicas and combines gradients. Sharded data parallelism partitions model state to save memory. Tensor parallelism splits operations within a layer; pipeline parallelism assigns groups of layers to stages. These methods trade memory for communication, synchronization, and scheduling complexity. Tensor-parallel collectives generally benefit from fast local interconnects, while pipeline utilization depends on enough microbatches to fill stages. Activation recomputation saves stored intermediates by repeating forward work during backward execution.

An illustrative 64-accelerator layout uses tensor parallel size four, pipeline size two, and data parallel size eight: 4 × 2 × 8 = 64. If each data replica processes two sequences per microbatch, accumulates 16 microbatches, and uses sequence length 2,048, one optimizer update covers 8 × 2 × 16 × 2,048 = 524,288 token positions. Tensor and pipeline factors do not multiply the sample count because they collaborate on the same samples. Masked or padded positions may reduce the number contributing to loss.

Monitor tokens per second, non-padding tokens per update, collective time, activation memory, gradient norms, and per-domain validation loss. A straggler can stall synchronous progress; larger batches may hide latency but change optimization. Diagnose whether the bottleneck is matrix compute, networking, input delivery, or imbalance before adding accelerators. Increased device count is useful only when it improves useful progress within the budget.

sections.title: 7. Checkpoint the experiment, not only its weights
paragraphs: A resumable checkpoint includes model and optimizer state, scheduler progress, random-number-generator state, step and token counters, sampler position, and the exact data/tokenizer/configuration manifest. PyTorch distributed checkpointing supports saving sharded state and loading with resharding, but application state still needs explicit handling. Never equate weight export for inference with a recoverable training checkpoint. A restart with fresh optimizer moments or repeated data can alter the experiment even if the loss initially looks plausible.

An operational design can write shards under a new checkpoint identifier, validate checksums and completeness, then publish a committed manifest. Readers ignore uncommitted versions. Test interruption during writing and test a full restore before the expensive run. For an illustrative 60-minute interval with failures uniformly distributed in time, expected lost work per failure is roughly 30 minutes, plus restart time. Shorter intervals reduce lost work but increase storage traffic. Asynchronous checkpointing helps only if its memory, staging, and I/O contention remain bounded.

sections.title: 8. Know what the fit cannot promise
paragraphs: Scaling fits describe observed statistical regularities, not guaranteed capability transitions. Token repetition, mixture changes, tokenizer changes, architecture changes, and different context lengths can move the frontier. Data-constrained scaling research explicitly models diminishing value from repeated exposure. Extra epochs can still help, but counting every repeated token as fresh information overstates the available diversity. Separately track unique tokens and total exposures.

Cross-entropy is an average over the evaluation distribution. Lower loss does not guarantee reliable tool use, calibrated uncertainty, factual freshness, or competence on a small critical subgroup. Keep task-specific gates and inspect distribution tails. A senior recommendation should present a candidate range, sensitivity to demand and data quality, a pilot experiment that could falsify the recommendation, and a stopping rule. That makes the proposed scaling decision auditable rather than rhetorical.

interview.question: You have 64 accelerators, 420B retained tokens, and a forecast of very heavy inference demand. A colleague proposes the largest model that fits and repeated training until the budget expires. How do you decide?
interview.answer: First validate the 420B count under the frozen tokenizer and measure unique coverage, mixture exposure, and contamination. Define quality and serving constraints, then fit small pilot runs across model sizes and training horizons. Translate sustained throughput into usable compute rather than using device peak specifications. Compare a training-efficient candidate with smaller candidates trained longer, while checking diminishing returns from repeated domains. Use inference demand ranges and measured serving behavior to estimate lifecycle costs. For execution, choose parallel factors whose product is 64, verify the global batch calculation, and test full checkpoint recovery including optimizer and sampler state. Select the cheapest candidate that passes the same clean task gates; do not assume the largest or the lowest pretraining loss automatically wins.
followUps: How would your choice change if inference demand fell by ten times?
Which experiment distinguishes poor mixture weights from insufficient model capacity?
How would you detect accidental replay after a checkpoint restore?
Why might a tokenizer change invalidate the existing scaling fit?

pitfalls: Treating raw crawl size, unique tokens, and training exposures as interchangeable.
Removing exact duplicates while leaving near-duplicate evaluation solutions in training.
Comparing token-level perplexity across incompatible tokenizers.
Presenting a tokens-per-parameter heuristic as a universal optimum.
Converting theoretical FLOPs directly into calendar time or dollars.
Multiplying global batch by tensor or pipeline parallel size.
Saving model weights without optimizer and data-progress state.
checklist: Freeze source manifests, tokenizer, packing rules, and evaluation partitions.
Audit quality-filter rejections and near-duplicate clusters by domain and language.
Report unique tokens, total exposures, mixture weights, and nominal passes.
Fit pilot runs at multiple sizes and horizons; validate on held-out runs.
Calculate training and lifetime serving budgets with explicit units and assumptions.
Profile the proposed topology and count loss-bearing tokens per optimizer update.
Interrupt and restore a complete checkpoint before committing the full run.
Gate scaling decisions on clean downstream tasks and subgroup results.

sources.note: Supports the parameter/data loss fit, approximate 6ND training compute, and approximately balanced parameter/token scaling; not a universal fixed ratio.

sources.title: Sardana et al. — Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal
sources.note: Supports including inference demand in model-size and training-data optimization.

sources.title: PyTorch — Distributed Checkpoint
sources.note: Documents distributed state saving/loading and resharding; application-level recovery state remains the training program's responsibility.

sources.title: Muennighoff et al. — Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models
sources.note: Supports modeling repeated data separately because its marginal training value diminishes.

sources.title: Kaplan et al. — Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
sources.note: Establishes empirical power-law relationships for language-model cross-entropy within studied regimes.

flashcards.front: Why is one trillion training tokens not a measure of one trillion tokens of novel information?
flashcards.back: Training tokens count exposures. Repeated documents, oversampled domains, and multiple epochs can inflate that count while unique coverage stays fixed, so track both exposure and diversity.

flashcards.front: What remains after retaining 80%, then 75%, then 70% of 1,000B tokens?
flashcards.back: 420B tokens: multiply conditional retention fractions, 1,000 × 0.8 × 0.75 × 0.7. Each percentage applies to the previous stage's output.

flashcards.front: Why does training-corpus deduplication not prove an evaluation is uncontaminated?
flashcards.back: A benchmark solution may appear only once in training, or as a paraphrase. Evaluation overlap needs separate checks and holdout design, beyond removing training duplicates.

flashcards.front: Why cannot perplexity be compared naively across tokenizers?
flashcards.back: The probability is averaged over different units and segmentations. A common normalization such as bits per byte and shared downstream tasks provides a more interpretable comparison.

flashcards.front: A 300B run allocates 20% to a 15B-token domain. How much repetition is expected?
flashcards.back: The domain receives 60B exposures, corresponding to four nominal passes. Sampling details affect coverage, but the calculation exposes oversampling that a mixture percentage alone hides.

flashcards.front: What does C ≈ 6ND estimate, and what does it leave out?
flashcards.back: Approximate dense-model training FLOPs for N parameters and D token exposures when parameter matrix multiplies dominate. Attention, recomputation, communication, and operational overhead require additional accounting.

flashcards.front: Under square-root scaling, how do parameters and tokens change when compute quadruples?
flashcards.back: Both double, so their product and approximate training FLOPs quadruple. This depends on the fitted frontier and is not a guarantee for every recipe.

flashcards.front: Why is a fixed tokens-per-parameter rule insufficient for a training plan?
flashcards.back: The optimum depends on data quality, repetition, architecture, schedule, and objective. It also ignores lifetime serving demand and hardware constraints.

flashcards.front: When can training a smaller model longer be economically sensible?
flashcards.back: When it reaches the required quality and reduced serving cost over enough lifetime tokens outweighs extra training cost. The comparison must include latency and memory constraints.

flashcards.front: How do you compute inference break-even for a model with extra training cost?
flashcards.back: Divide extra training cost by per-token inference savings in consistent units. The result is lifetime tokens, assuming comparable quality and a valid per-token cost model.

flashcards.front: Which parallel dimensions multiply the number of samples in a global batch?
flashcards.back: Data-parallel replicas multiply distinct samples; tensor and pipeline workers collaborate on those samples. Include microbatch size and gradient-accumulation count, then account for masking.

flashcards.front: What is missing from a weights-only checkpoint for training recovery?
flashcards.back: Optimizer moments, scheduler progress, random state, sampler position, counters, and experiment manifests. Missing these can change optimization or replay data after restart.

flashcards.front: With hourly checkpoints, what is approximate lost work per uniformly timed failure?
flashcards.back: About 30 minutes on average, plus restart overhead. More frequent saves lower wasted work but consume I/O and potentially memory or compute resources.

flashcards.front: How do you make a scaling-law prediction defensible in an interview?
flashcards.back: State its training regime and units, fit multiple pilot sizes and horizons, validate on held-out runs, analyze sensitivity, and require clean task-specific quality gates before scaling.
